doc.title: Bobby Watson interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, January 19, 1996

chapter: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers
title: Improvisation by the whole rhythm section
summary: Everyone improvises from the start; comping, bass lines and drum cues work as a team and soloists trust those around them.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah. You want me, you got me. And so I never wrote drum parts out again, and I still don’t to this day. I may give a trumpet part. And so that’s why this improvisation you’re saying begins immediately when you have artists that are in that spirit of creating so that when they’re comping, they’re actually playing little counter melodies and there’s this voice leading and all the chords, and if you just take away all the chords and just listen to what’s on top, you should hear the little counter melodies flowing behind you and in the bass, if you really just isolate the bass you’ll hear how he’s composing on his bass lines. His melodies that he’s walking, that’s how they’re able to keep walking all them bars, they’re improvising. They’re soloing on the bass. And so it’s like everything is in motion. If you’ve got guys that are playing the stuff over and over the way you wrote it, that’s not jazz. The hardest thing is to get people to realize that you’re improvising from the word go. You know you’ve picked the voicings. You picked the rhythm. When you want to hear the drums, you guys hook up on something behind the soloist to push him on. And that’s the whole thing about it. It’s a team ball. You pass. And when you hear the guy go over to the cymbal, you can almost hear it coming. You know he’ll do a roll and it’s like when you turn the corner, you know you put the signal light on about 50 feet before. So you hear the signal light come on, and you hear him slow down to make the curve. So you hear these things in the music. So you as a soloist you’re going, okay, they’re going to curve and you go right with them. And they see the same thing. When they see my shoulder start going like this and I start stomping my foot, they go oh there he goes. And they start feeding me little stuff you know? And we all just move out together. It’s the hardest thing that Art taught me, he said, “When you start to blow, man, you’ve got to trust the guys around you and you all move out together.” And we build, you know, just like that.
